title: Three days after losing Congress, Trump hands the White House to Stephen Miller. The plan for it was already written
dek: Susie Wiles resigned Thursday night; Miller takes over Monday. He has spent the past seven months with Russ Vought cataloguing what the president can do without Congress, and the Democrats who take Congress in January say they will start with him.
body:
Susie Wiles handed President Donald Trump her resignation on Thursday night, three days after Republicans lost both chambers of Congress [1][2]. On Friday afternoon, in a Truth Social post, Trump announced that Stephen Miller, his deputy chief of staff for policy and “one of my most trusted advisors,” would be White House chief of staff from Monday [3][4]. Wiles, he wrote, would move to his political operation [3][5].

The job Miller inherits is the one with the office next to the president’s. The chief of staff runs the building, decides who and what reaches the president, and manages his time; insiders call it the gatekeeper, because the role largely controls the flow of information [8]. The man taking it has spent the past seven months, by Reuters’ account, working out what the president can do with no Congress at all [6].

## What happened, hour by hour

Wiles’s resignation came Thursday night, a person familiar with the conversation told The Associated Press [1]. CBS News’s sources tied it to the midterm defeat, and said she had planned to stay through the lame-duck session, which would have ended her tenure around the turn of the year. Trump moved that forward [2]. “Today is my last day as White House Chief of Staff,” she posted on X on Friday afternoon, calling the job “the honor of a lifetime” [3][2].

Trump, leaving the White House for an event at Cape Canaveral, told reporters Wiles had done “a great job” and that the change was “not because of the election. It’s just time” [1][3]. “Sometimes in life you have to make moves,” he said [3]. He described Miller as “very good politically” and a “great manager,” and said of the midterms, “I wasn’t on the ballot” [1][2].

Miller’s statement, on X, said it had been “the privilege of my lifetime” to serve on Trump’s team from the first day and that he was “honored beyond words” [3]. He thanked Wiles and described the mission as fighting “with all of our soul” for the president and “this magnificent Republic” [2]. The X account of Trump’s political operation posted a black-and-white photograph of him captioned “It’s Miller time” [3]. Communications director Steven Cheung called him “a Trump OG, someone who has been with the President since the very beginning” [17].

Wiles leaves after 21 months, the longest of Trump’s five chiefs of staff across two terms and the first woman in the job [9][1]. She ran his 2024 campaign and had held the post since his first day back in office [2]. Her year was eventful. In December she gave Vanity Fair 11 interviews in which she said Trump has “an alcoholic’s personality,” called Vice President JD Vance a decade-long “conspiracy theorist,” and said Pam Bondi, the attorney general at the time, “completely whiffed” on the Epstein files. She called the resulting article a “disingenuously framed hit piece” but did not deny the quotes; Trump said she was “right” and called her “fantastic” [14][1].

## The man, in one paragraph

Miller, 41, joined the 2016 campaign in January of that year as a speechwriter and policy adviser and is the longest-serving of Trump’s aides [1][8]. In the first term he shaped the travel ban and the 2018 zero-tolerance policy that separated families at the border [8]. In the second he has been deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser, the architect of the deportation program, a leading member of the anti-fraud task force aimed at benefit programs, and, in October, a leader of the decision to suspend Microsoft and other companies from a green card program [1]. He is also, the AP noted, the aide who called Democrats “extremists, freaks and America-hating lunatics” during the campaign and promoted unfounded fraud theories about the counts in California and Alaska [1]. A fuller profile, and the story of the 2006 clip that has followed him since Friday night, are in companion pieces.

## The plan that was already written

The appointment is less a change of direction than the confirmation of one. Reuters reported on November 1, two days before the vote, that Miller and budget director Russell Vought had been working with the White House counsel’s office since April on a list of actions Trump could take without Congress if Democrats won [6]. Federal agencies had submitted proposals and legal reviews [6]. On the list, according to Reuters’ sources: tighter rules on visas for foreign students and temporary workers; new tariffs on imported critical minerals and wind turbines; measures aimed at housing and construction costs; and, from Vought, a review of which priorities can run on money Congress has already appropriated, plus a change to federal grant rules that would give political appointees more say over which programs get funds [6]. White House counsel Will Scharf’s team was examining how far the president’s authority could be pushed and how to defend it in court, and the White House planned to seek Justice Department opinions, including one that could let Trump claim executive privilege over his communications with private advisers [6].

Trump has said how he expects the next two years to go. “I guess I’ll become Mr. Veto,” he told the New York Post’s podcast, predicting vetoes for “a month or two” and then, “at some point, we’ll probably make deals” [6]. He has also pointed to the Supreme Court’s June 29 decision in Trump v. Slaughter, which overruled the 1935 Humphrey’s Executor precedent by a 6-3 vote and lets a president remove the heads of independent agencies at will, the Federal Reserve excepted [13]. The case, he told CBS, “gives the president tremendous powers that it never had before” [5].

Fox News framed the switch from Wiles to Miller as “a major tactical shift for governing without Congress” [5]. One official told Fox the administration would keep governing “without Congress, as they’ve been doing” [5]. Another, asked about Democratic oversight, said that if “crazed Democrats” wanted to politicize investigations, “they should be reminded that we still control the federal government and all of its powers” [5]. Spokeswoman Lauren Bis said the White House was “willing to work with anyone” [5]. One House Republican told Fox a different worry: “I’ve been concerned about that for two years,” meaning that Trump might cut populist deals with Democrats instead [5].

## What Democrats said in the first six hours

Rep. Robert Garcia of California, in line to chair the House Oversight Committee in January, posted a letter within hours. Miller, he wrote, “is the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorized our communities”; Oversight Democrats “will continue to investigate Miller for his conduct”; and “Stephen Miller should lawyer up” [10][11]. Todd Blanche, of the Justice Department, answered on television: “I’m his lawyer,” and called it “so disgusting” that Democrats had not waited “till the week is out” to lay their cards on the table [15].

Hakeem Jeffries, the likely next speaker, called Miller “a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands” [7][11]. Miller’s presence in government, he wrote, “should be eradicated like a malignant tumor. Fire him today” [11]. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said Trump “couldn’t have made a worse choice” and had “learned nothing from his historic defeat”; “Our Democratic majorities will fight him every step of the way” [11][7]. Al Jazeera reported that Democrats are widely expected to open investigations into Miller’s White House role once they take both chambers [8].

Republicans divided on tone rather than substance. Steve Bannon told NBC News that Miller “knows the key issues and is a true believer,” and that he “gets parachuted in and takes immediate control” [16]. Mick Mulvaney, a first-term chief of staff, said the choice sends “a clear message” to the incoming majority [7]. One Republican lobbyist told The Hill the promotion would only worsen relations between the White House and Capitol Hill [7]. Trump, on a recent call with an ally, praised Miller as an aide who does not just tell him what he wants to hear, and the ally said Miller would be combative with Congress on investigations in particular [16].

## The numbers behind the fight

The voters who produced the Democratic majorities had already passed judgment on Miller’s signature program. In the AP Voter Poll, about six in ten said the administration’s immigration enforcement had gone too far; about two in ten said it had not gone far enough and about two in ten called it about right [12]. About seven in ten wanted Congress to provide more checks and balances on the presidency, and about six in ten disapproved of Trump’s handling of the job [12]. The Washington Post called Tuesday the largest shift to the left in half a century, and the Miller appointment “a gamble” on reinforcing the agenda and perhaps moving further right [4].

## What changes Monday, and what does not

How the new title changes Miller’s actual influence is unclear even to the people reporting on it; Al Jazeera noted that it was “not immediately clear” how the role would alter his standing with Trump [8]. He already sat, according to a person familiar with the process, in the small group of staffers who approve every executive order [18]. Whether Wiles’s deputies stay on is not known [2]. Trump has signaled more Cabinet departures in an interview with CBS’s 60 Minutes that airs Sunday [15].

Three dates are fixed. Miller takes over Monday, November 9 [3]. Democrats take the House and the Senate in January [8]. And the House Oversight Committee, under Garcia, has already said whose name is first on its list [10].
